gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured idle draw (inverter on, no load): The Solar Lab measured 8 W on the Jackery HomePower 3000, about 15 W on the BLUETTI Elite 300, about 18 W on the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (Anker claims 9 W), about 22 W on the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra and about 27 W on the DELTA 3 Max, and it estimated over 70 W on the Anker SOLIX F3800. Over a 24-hour boondocking day, that idle draw alone uses between 6% and 44% of the battery.
standout_why: I read both cited rivals in full. SolutionEnergy (solutionenergy.com/portable-power/rv, dated 2026-10-03) says it made no measurements. Its only idle figure is Anker's own claim of 9 W for the C2000 Gen 2, and every runtime on the page comes from an assumed 0.85 usable-energy factor. QuietTechReport (dated 2026-08-22) says it did no hands-on testing. It repeats the makers' 30 dB claims and calculates runtimes from an assumed 85% efficiency. I could not read TechRadar's page because it came back cut off after the title. Neither cited rival gives an idle draw measured by a named tester, a usable-capacity test or an efficiency test for any candidate.
decides: The measurements back the Jackery HomePower 3000, one of ChatGPT's own picks, as the 3 kWh choice for multi-day dry camping. With the inverter left on to run a fridge, its 8 W idle uses about 192 Wh a day (6% of 3,072 Wh). The DELTA 3 Ultra's 22 W uses about 528 Wh a day (17%). They also count against the Anker SOLIX F3800 (our 50 A row) for boondocking: at over 70 W, idle alone would use about 1,680 Wh a day and empty its 3,840 Wh in about 55 hours with no load. Among the 2 kWh units, Anker's '9 W idle' marketing for the C2000 Gen 2 measured at about 18 W, which is about 432 Wh a day (21%). The DELTA 3 Max measured 27 W, about 648 Wh a day (32%). Load efficiency also cuts the real energy available. Notebookcheck got only about 1,600 Wh (79%) out of the C2000 Gen 2 at a fridge-sized 200 W load. Outdoor Gear Lab measured 3,790 Wh (93%) from the DELTA Pro 3. The page should use measured figures in place of a flat 85%.

findings.label: Idle draw, inverter on (The Solar Lab)
findings.source_title: Jackery HomePower 3000 Review: Is Jackery's First "HomePower" Unit a Good Purchase?
findings.note: The page says "an idle consumption of just 8 watts" and calls it the best The Solar Lab has seen from a large station. The page has no byline or article date. My arithmetic: 8 W × 24 h = 192 Wh/day, 6.25% of the rated 3,072 Wh.

findings.label: Idle draw, efficiency, surge, AC charge time (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: about 15 W idle; about 86% efficiency; surge up to 3,900 W; 0–100% wall charge in about 2 h 44 min
findings.source_title: The Solar Lab BLUETTI Elite 300 review
findings.note: "We measured the idle rate around 15W." The page gives no test load for the efficiency figure. Its own estimate of 'about three days' on idle does not match 15 W: 3,014 Wh ÷ 15 W ≈ 8.4 days, and The Solar Lab's comparison page says 8.3 days. My arithmetic: 15 × 24 = 360 Wh/day. No author or date on the page.

findings.label: Idle draw, efficiency, surge, AC charge time (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: about 18 W idle (Anker advertises 9 W); about 89% efficiency; surges to 6,000 W in short bursts; 0–100% on AC in about 88 min
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 Review: One of the Best Anker Power Stations?
findings.note: "idle draw sat closer to 18W per hour" against Anker's advertised "9W idle draw". The page gives no load for the efficiency test. AC plus solar charged it in 58 min. My arithmetic: 18 × 24 = 432 Wh/day, 21% of 2,048 Wh. No author or date on the page.

findings.label: Usable energy at low and high load, charge efficiency, noise (Notebookcheck)
findings.value: about 1,600 Wh (just under 79%) at about 200 W AC load; about 1,850 Wh (about 90%) at 1,800 W; 87% AC charge efficiency (about 2,350 Wh drawn from the wall); about 35 dB at 1 m under high load
findings.source_title: 11.6 kg lighter than its predecessor: Powerstation Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 review
findings.note: By Marcus Schwarten, published 2026-02-24 and updated 2026-10-05. Notebookcheck tested a European 230 V unit, which the review says differs slightly from the US model. The 200 W case is close to an overnight fridge-and-lights load in a trailer.

findings.label: Measured energy out (Outdoor Gear Lab)
findings.value: 3,790 Wh of 4,096 Wh rated (93%); average charge rate 1,293 Wh/h, peaking above 1,600 W; full charge in 3.2 h
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 Review | Outdoor Gear Lab
findings.note: By Kenji Mowrey, dated 2026-01-13. The review does not state the test load. It gives no idle draw or noise measurement.

findings.label: Discharge capacity across cycles (Digital Trends)
findings.value: 3.7 kWh on average; about 5 kWh drawn from the wall to charge from 0%; about 3 h for 0–100%
findings.source_title: This brute of a power station will power almost anything — even A/C (EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 review)
findings.note: By Simon Sage, 2024-06-25. Despite the headline, the review reports no air-conditioner test.

findings.label: Near-maximum load run and surge (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: 60 min at a sustained 3,650 W (about 89% efficiency); held 5,100 W for nearly a minute before shutting down; 120 V AC charge in about 2 h 54 min (2 h 20 min advertised)
findings.source_title: The Solar Lab EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 review
findings.note: The review gives no idle draw. No author or date on the page.

findings.label: Idle draw, efficiency, AC charge time (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: about 22 W idle; about 82% efficiency; 0–100% on a household outlet in about 2 h; about 4 h on solar in ideal conditions
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Ultra vs BLUETTI Elite 300: Which Portable Power Station is Better?
findings.note: The Solar Lab's standalone DELTA 3 Ultra review (https://www.thesolarlab.com/review/ecoflow-delta-3-ultra, read 2026-11-17) gives the same figures: about 82%, "roughly 22 watts" idle, about 5.7 days on idle and a 2 h charge. The comparison page puts the Elite 300 at 15 W idle (about 8.3 days). My arithmetic: 22 × 24 = 528 Wh/day, 17% of 3,072 Wh. No author or date on either page.

findings.label: Idle draw, efficiency, charge time (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: about 27 W idle; 79% efficiency; 0–100% on AC in 68 min; over 4 h on solar
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Review: A Step Forward or a Step Sideways?
findings.note: "we calculated the idle consumption at about 27 watts". The page gives no test load. My arithmetic: 27 × 24 = 648 Wh/day, 32% of 2,048 Wh. No author or date on the page.

findings.label: Idle draw, estimated (The Solar Lab)
findings.source_title: The Solar Lab: idle consumption explainer
findings.note: This figure was estimated, not metered. During a 24-hour blackout test with only a fridge and a router running, The Solar Lab compared the battery drain with the expected use and worked back to the idle draw ('napkin math'). A search snippet attributed a figure of about 80 W to another Solar Lab page, but I did not open that page, so I have used 70 W. My arithmetic: 70 × 24 = 1,680 Wh/day, 44% of 3,840 Wh, so the battery would be empty in about 55 h on idle alone.

findings.label: High-load run, surge, AC charge time (The Solar Lab)
findings.value: 37 min at 5,100 W (about 84% efficiency); 8,000 W held for about 2–3 s; 7,200 W for about 10 s; 120 V wall charge in 2 h 35 min (2 h 25 min claimed)
findings.source_title: Putting the Anker F3800 Power Station to the Test: What Can It ACTUALLY Handle?
findings.note: This was a garage test with an air compressor, a car lift and a table saw. No air conditioner was tested. No author or date on the page.

findings.label: AC charge time checked (Notebookcheck)
findings.value: full charge at 2,400 W AC input in about 1.5 h, matching BLUETTI's claim
findings.source_title: Bluetti AC200L hands-on review: Fast-charging power station delivers convincing results
findings.note: By Polly Allcock, 2024-08-05, updated 2026-02-18. Notebookcheck tested the 230 V UK/EU/AU unit. Its efficiency (93%) and self-consumption (12 W) figures are BLUETTI's, not measurements. About 45 min running a 2,400 W device 'roughly tallies' with what the reviewer saw.
